items.content:
RT @MonThreat: 🚨Threat Actor Claims 882M Pinduoduo User Records for Sale on Darkweb

A listing on an underground forum claims to offer a massive dataset allegedly stolen from Pinduoduo, one of China's largest e-commerce platforms. The post alleges that the database contains records for 882.19 million users, including sensitive personal information and detailed transaction histories.

According to the listing, the exposed data includes user identifiers, names, mobile phone numbers, email addresses, and login methods (such as WeChat or SMS). The dataset reportedly also contains granular financial and behavioral data, such as:
- Order history and status (paid, cancelled, refunded)
- Payment method breakdowns (WeChat Pay, Alipay)
- Total goods amounts and refund values in CNY
- Wallet balances and 'pay later' credit limits
- Shipping details and carrier information
- Review activity and counterfeit claim statistics

The actor is demanding $1,400 for the full dataset, payable in various cryptocurrencies including BTC, ETH, LTC, SOL, USDT, and XMR. The post includes sample rows of data to demonstrate the scope of the alleged breach, showing specific user profiles with registration dates ranging from 2016 to 2026.

Pinduoduo, operated by PDD Holdings, is a major Chinese online marketplace known for its low-cost consumer goods and social commerce model. It serves hundreds of millions of active users globally. If authentic, the exposure of such a vast amount of PII and financial behavior data could facilitate targeted phishing campaigns, identity theft, and fraud against Chinese consumers.

The threat actor behind this post has limited public history, with previous activity consisting primarily of automated probe posts on other forums, suggesting this may be a new or opportunistic operation rather than a high-profile ransomware group. At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified by Pinduoduo or security researchers.

items.content:
RT @InsiderGeo: NEW: A major cross-border investigation has uncovered how Russian and Ukrainian nationals, including individuals linked to Vladimir Putin, Ramzan Kadyrov, Russian state companies and pro-Kremlin networks, allegedly obtained Romanian identity documents using fraudulent citizenship certificates and fictitious addresses.

The investigation, conducted over more than six months by CU SENS, Public Record, The Kyiv Independent, Le Monde, Follow the Money and The Investigative Center of Ján Kuciak, examined more than 50 court cases in Romania.

Among the individuals identified:

- Kirill Seleznev, a Russian businessman, former senior Gazprom executive and internationally sanctioned individual described as close to Vladimir Putin. His Romanian civil-status registrations were annulled by a Bucharest court this year.

- Mairbek Abdulazizov, a Russian national reportedly connected to Ramzan Kadyrov's inner circle. He allegedly obtained Romanian documents using a Ukrainian passport and a citizenship certificate that Romanian court records describe as inauthentic.

- Dmitrii Rudenko, a former head of a Russian state-owned company involved in the production of explosives, who allegedly obtained Romanian documents using a fraudulent citizenship certificate.

- Nurutdin Dadaev, a Russian national from Dagestan identified by Ukraine as a so-called “thief-in-law” and listed by Russia as a terrorist and extremist.

The investigation also identified four wanted leaders of the Allatra movement, who are being investigated in Ukraine for treason and allegedly obtained Romanian citizenship using fraudulent documents.

A key part of the scheme allegedly ran through the Romanian commune of Vârfu Câmpului, near the borders with Moldova and Ukraine. The locality had around 3,000 residents in 2011, but more than 12,000 people now have their registered domicile there. In some cases, thousands of people were registered at a single address.

The investigation describes a network of intermediaries, property owners and public officials allegedly facilitating fictitious residence registrations in exchange for money. In March 2025, five local and population-records officials appeared before judges over allegations of bribery and computer fraud.

The trail also led to Chișinău, where two Moldovan notaries, Carolina Hanganu and Andrei Șumcov, appeared in documents connected to Romanian citizenship and identity cases. Hanganu legalised documents for 12 Russian or Ukrainian nationals whose Romanian papers are now being challenged, while Șumcov prepared powers of attorney used in the process.

Romanian authorities are now seeking to annul documents obtained through allegedly fraudulent citizenship certificates. However, the investigations remain ongoing, and many of the individuals identified continue to move freely within Europe.

Back on September 4, I publicly raised these concerns, despite the risks of exposing information I knew. Since then, I have also discussed the issue with several journalists and officials. I am glad this investigation is finally bringing attention to it. :)

items.content:
RT @0x4D31: a couple of things worth remembering whenever you hear another “it’s over” take about AI:

1. people have different incentives. some are selling something, some are invested in a particular outcome, and some genuinely believe what they’re saying. often it’s a mix of all three, and it’s hard to tell how much those incentives shape their takes.

2. being an expert in a technology, even one you helped invent, doesn’t automatically make you right about its broader implications. the real world is far more complex than a single tweet, headline, or interview.

so yeah, do your own research and form your own opinions before freaking out over every confident prediction about AI :))

items.content:
RT @ayushagarwal027: A Linux socket costs about 3,300 bytes of kernel memory, even when idle. A userland network stack in Rust, together with a custom runtime, reached 16 million servers on one 10 GB VM. 🦀

The article "15 million web servers on one VM" by @kaptekoguid (kapteko) is a humorous but technically clear experiment: run one web server for every person on the planet, starting with 15 million on a single VM with 10 GB of RAM and one CPU core.

The path, step by step:
→ A plain C server hits the port limit first. AnyIP, which lets a machine listen on a whole subnet, solves the addressing
→ Each process then costs about 1.5 MB, so 15 million would need around 20 TB of RAM. The answer is a custom runtime that runs the servers as sandboxed guests in one process, using LFI for isolation, with about 16 bytes of scheduling state per guest. That runtime comes from earlier articles by the same author
→ The kernel finding: a socket call allocates about 3,300 bytes whether the socket is active, listening or doing nothing. The post breaks down 3,384 bytes: tcp_sock 2,240, socket_alloc 768, file 184 and dentry 192. The author's first assumption that idle listeners would cost zero memory was wrong, and the post says so

The fix is to go lower in the network stack. smoltcp, a Rust TCP/IP stack that needs no heap allocation, handles the protocol in userland. Packet I/O comes through TUN or TAP, DPDK, or AF_XDP:
→ DPDK takes the network device from the OS and uses a busy-looping core
→ AF_XDP leaves the device with the kernel and uses an eBPF filter to route packets to userspace, so SSH keeps working

The results, from the author's benchmark:
→ With the kernel network stack, memory runs out at around 2.5 million servers, and requests per second drop as the count grows
→ With smoltcp, an idle server costs about 620 bytes and an active one about 1 KB, and the run reached 16 million servers
→ DPDK is fastest, with AF_XDP just behind

🔗 https://t.co/osHVMuc0NO

items.content:
RT @elder_plinius: WOAH! turns out you can effectively "abliterate" models (like the new Inkling-2-Mini) simply by changing 10 words in the dictionary 🤯

the working name is "Vocab Surgery," and it resulted in the refusal rate dropping to near-zero on the 800+ prompts I tested, with negligible capability loss 😱

here's how:

we made zero changes to any of the 26.4 billion parameters in the attention, MLP, router, or normalization layers—just changed a handful of rows in two matrices:

> embedding matrix (how the model READS tokens):
Modified 7 rows out of 201,024. Each refusal token's embedding was shifted 90% toward its compliance counterpart:
"cannot" → shifted toward "can"
" refuse" → shifted toward " provide"
" unable" → shifted toward " able"
" harmful" → shifted toward " helpful"
" illegal" → shifted toward " legal"

> unembedding matrix (how the model WRITES tokens):
Modified 10 rows. Scaled those same 7 refusal tokens + 3 safety tokens ("safety", " safety", "Safety") down to 10% of their original weight — meaning the model's probability of outputting those tokens drops ~10x.

in other words, the brain is entirely intact, we just messed with the ears and mouth a bit! that means more coherence and less capability loss 🙌 

not to mention this process is FAST...in this case taking <2 minutes on my MacBook ⚡️
